alignment.note: The Greek places the object pronoun αὐτόν before the verb εἶδον, and Latin follows the Greek order with the verb-first arrangement (viderunt eum). Syriac fuses the object pronominal suffix onto the verb (ܚܙܐܘܗܝ, 'they-saw-him'), a single morphological word reflecting standard Aramaic synthetic syntax.
Syriac index 2 carries both verb and object suffix; the verbal stem aligns with εἶδον / viderunt.

Greek uses a single aorist passive ἐταράχθησαν ('they were troubled'); Latin renders it periphrastically with participle plus auxiliary (conturbati sunt); Syriac uses a simple peal perfect ܘܕܚܠܘ from d-kh-l ('they feared/were afraid'), which leans toward fear rather than agitation, a slight lexical shift in emotional nuance.

Greek marks the subject change with the article + postpositive δέ (ὁ δέ, 'but he'); Latin uses the simple connective Et; Syriac has no separate equivalent here, beginning the clause with the temporal phrase. The contrastive force of δέ is flattened in both versions.

Greek εὐθύς and Latin statim are single adverbs ('immediately'); Syriac employs the idiomatic temporal phrase ܒܪ ܫܥܬܗ ('son of its hour', i.e. 'at that very moment'), a characteristic Aramaic periphrasis for immediacy.
Greek aorist ἐλάλησεν; Latin perfect periphrasis locutus est; Syriac peal perfect ܡܠܠ — all 'he spoke'.
Greek preposition + genitive μετ' αὐτῶν and Latin cum eis correspond to the Syriac ܥܡܗܘܢ, which fuses preposition and pronominal suffix into one synthetic form.

Greek shifts to the historic present λέγει ('he says'), a Markan stylistic vividism; both Latin (dixit) and Syriac (the perfect prefixed within ܘܐܡܪ) normalise this to a past tense, smoothing the tense alternation typical of the secondary versions.
Greek dative αὐτοῖς, Latin dative eis with following colon, and Syriac ܠܗܘܢ (preposition + suffix) all express 'to them'.
Greek imperative θαρσεῖτε, Latin Confidite, and Syriac ethpaal imperative ܐܬܠܒܒܘ (from l-b-b, 'take heart') all convey 'take courage'.
The emphatic self-identification ἐγώ εἰμι ('I am [he]') is matched by Latin ego sum and the Syriac doubled ܐܢܐ ܐܢܐ, the regular Aramaic copular construction for the predicate 'I am'.
Prohibition μὴ φοβεῖσθε rendered by Latin nolite timere and Syriac ܠܐ ܬܕܚܠܘܢ ('do not fear'), all negated second-person plural commands.
